meta.disclaimer: Savanna Explorer planning guides are written in our own words based on publicly available official sources. Visa rules, entry requirements, fees, and health guidance change without notice. Always verify requirements with your government's travel advisory and the relevant immigration authority before booking or travelling. Park fees and accommodation rates quoted are indicative only.

sections.title: Where to Go
sections.body:
Namibia rewards travellers who venture far from the beaten track. Etosha National Park in the north is the crown jewel — a vast salt pan ringed by waterholes where elephant, lion, cheetah, and black rhino converge in the dry season. The best waterholes for evening viewing are Okaukuejo and Halali, both floodlit after dark. To the south, Sossusvlei in the Namib-Naukluft National Park delivers some of the most photographed landscapes on Earth: towering apricot dunes, the ghostly Deadvlei with its ancient dead camelthorn trees, and the infinite gravel plains of the world's oldest desert. The Skeleton Coast stretches along the Atlantic, bleak and hauntingly beautiful, with shipwrecks half-buried in fog and desert-adapted lions patrolling remote beaches.

Damaraland in northwest Namibia is one of Africa's finest off-the-beaten-track regions — purple mountain ranges, ancestral Himba communities, and petroglyph art at Twyfelfontein (a UNESCO World Heritage Site). Free-roaming desert-adapted elephants and black rhino are tracked here on foot by community conservancy scouts. Fish River Canyon in the south is Africa's largest canyon, and the site of a challenging multi-day hiking trail open from May to September. The Zambezi Region in the northeast opens into lush floodplain wetlands that feel more like East Africa than the Namib, with sable antelope, hippo, and crocodile in channels that connect to Botswana's Chobe.
bullets: Etosha: three rest camps (Okaukuejo, Halali, Namutoni) with floodlit night waterholes for elephant, lion, and rhino viewing
Sossusvlei & Deadvlei: sunrise dune climbs are best from NamibRand or Sesriem camp; gate opens at sunrise sharp
Skeleton Coast (restricted northern zone): requires a licensed fly-in or guided tour — no independent access
Twyfelfontein: 2,000+ Khoisan rock engravings dating back 6,000 years; UNESCO World Heritage Site
Fish River Canyon hike: 85km, 5-day trail bookable through NWR (May–Sep only; medical certificate required)

sections.title: Where to Stay
sections.body:
Namibia offers an exceptional range of accommodation from five-star desert lodges to basic national park campsites. At the top end, private lodges in the NamibRand Nature Reserve — including Wolwedans Dune Lodge and Little Kulala — are among Africa's most sustainably designed properties, using local stone, reclaimed timber, and solar power to minimise their footprint while maximising the landscape. The views are extraordinary and the sense of solitude complete. Mid-range self-catering farmstays (guestfarms) are unique to Namibia and offer home-cooked dinners, swimming pools, and excellent personal hospitality, typically from NAD 1,500–3,500 per person per night including dinner and breakfast.

Namibia Wildlife Resorts (NWR) operates all rest camps inside national parks, including Etosha's three main camps (Okaukuejo, Halali, Namutoni). Options range from powered campsites to fully equipped chalets. Bookings open six months in advance and fill quickly for July–September — reserving as early as possible is essential. The communal conservancy lodges in Damaraland and Kaokoland, such as Etendeka and Palmwag, directly benefit local communities and provide a deeply authentic wildlife encounter. For budget travellers, the Trans-Kalahari corridor has several well-run private campsites between Windhoek and Botswana.
bullets: NWR Etosha camps: book via nwr.com.na — 6 months in advance; peak season (Jul–Sep) fills within hours of opening
Private desert lodges: NamibRand, Wolwedans, Sossusvlei Lodge — luxury with near-zero footprint
Guestfarms on C-roads: sociable dinners, safe parking for self-drivers, typically NAD 1,500–3,500 pps dinner-bed-breakfast
Communal conservancy camps (Damaraland, Kaokoland) — revenue distributed directly to local communities
Wild camping is restricted in Namibia; use designated NWR or conservancy campsites to avoid fines

sections.title: Best Times to Visit
sections.body:
The best wildlife viewing in Etosha runs from June through October when the dry season forces animals to concentrate around waterholes. Daytime temperatures reach 20–28°C and evenings can be crisp enough for a jacket. This is peak season — accommodation books out many months in advance and self-drive routes are busiest. The Namib Desert is visitable year-round, but sunrise and sunset photography on the Sossusvlei dunes is best from April–October when the air is clearest and haze is minimal.

November through April brings Namibia's summer — scattered rains green the gravel plains and offer excellent photography of newborn springbok and oryx against vivid red soil. Etosha is still productive in early summer but dense vegetation makes game spotting harder. The Skeleton Coast is best avoided in summer when heavy Atlantic fog and cold winds persist throughout the day. Swakopmund on the coast provides a cool base year-round thanks to the Benguela Current — even in January daytime temperatures rarely exceed 22°C. The shoulder months of April–May and September–October offer an excellent balance: solid game viewing, moderate temperatures, and fewer fellow travellers at waterholes.
bullets: Jun–Oct: peak game viewing at Etosha; cold desert nights can drop below 5°C in July — pack warm layers
Dec–Mar: green season — vivid dunes, wildflowers in the Namaqualand, migratory birds arrive
Apr–May and Sep–Oct: shoulder season — good wildlife, fewer crowds, better value on accommodation
Sossusvlei: accessible year-round; NamibRand gate opens at sunrise and closes at sunset — no exceptions
Swakopmund: cool coastal base year-round; use as a midpoint between Etosha and Sossusvlei circuits

sections.title: Entry & Visa
sections.body:
Significant changes came into effect from 1 April 2025: visitors from the UK, USA, EU member states, Australia, and Canada who previously entered Namibia visa-free now require either an e-visa applied for in advance or a visa-on-arrival at designated entry points. The visa-on-arrival costs approximately N$1,200–1,600 for a single entry and is available at Hosea Kutako International Airport (Windhoek), Walvis Bay Airport, and major land border crossings. However, the official Namibian e-visa portal at eservices.mhaiss.gov.na is strongly recommended to avoid potential queues and delays at the border — particularly important if connecting to a domestic or international flight.

South African passport holders and most other SADC nationals continue to enter visa-free for up to 90 days. A passport valid for at least six months beyond your departure date and at least one blank page for visa stamps is required at all borders. Yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if arriving from a yellow fever endemic country. Malaria prophylaxis is strongly recommended for travel to the Zambezi Region and northern areas; the rest of Namibia is generally low risk.
bullets: UK, US, EU, AU, CA: e-visa required from 1 Apr 2025 — apply in advance at eservices.mhaiss.gov.na
Visa-on-arrival: available at Windhoek airport (~N$1,200–1,600 single entry, cash or card)
South Africa and most SADC nationals: visa-free up to 90 days — confirm at mha.gov.na
Passport valid 6+ months beyond departure; at least one blank visa page required
Yellow fever certificate needed if arriving from endemic countries; malaria risk in Zambezi/Caprivi region

sections.title: Self-Drive Tips
sections.body:
Namibia is one of the world's great self-drive destinations — roughly 45,000km of roads connect the country's highlights, and the vast majority are navigable in a standard 2WD saloon outside of the rainy season. The main arteries (B1 Windhoek–Ondangwa, B2 Windhoek–Swakopmund) are tar and well-maintained. Gravel C-roads require more care — a high-clearance 4x4 or robust SUV is recommended for Damaraland, Kaokoland, the Skeleton Coast, and at any time after heavy rain. Drive on the left; the recommended speed on Namibian gravel is 80km/h, and many experienced drivers suggest 60–70km/h to avoid tyre blowouts from sharp stones. Never swerve suddenly on gravel at speed — it causes rollovers.

Fuel discipline is critical outside Windhoek and Swakopmund. Towns can be 200km or more apart in the northwest and south. Carry at least 20 litres of reserve fuel and 10 litres of water per person on any remote route. A paper road map or offline GPS (MapsMe Namibia is well-regarded; download before leaving Windhoek) is essential — cell signal disappears quickly beyond town perimeters. Share your planned route with your accommodation and check in at each destination. Most lodges and NWR camps will advise on current road conditions and flag any known hazards.
bullets: 2WD fine for B1, B2, and most C-roads in dry season; 4x4 essential for Kaokoland, Skeleton Coast, Damaraland
Gravel driving rule: keep below 80km/h; swerving at speed is the leading cause of tourist rollovers
Fuel up at every opportunity on remote routes; carry 20L reserve; note fuel stations are rarely open after 8pm
Download offline maps before leaving Windhoek — MapsMe Namibia or Google Maps offline both work well
NWR gates close at sunset — plan distances carefully; distances in Namibia are deceptively large on a map

sections.title: Cape Town & Winelands
sections.body:
Few cities on Earth match Cape Town for sheer geographic drama — the flat-topped mass of Table Mountain rising 1,085 metres above a city of sea, vine-covered valleys, and two converging oceans. The V&A Waterfront provides a stylish city base with restaurants, museums, and a working harbour within walking distance. The Bo-Kaap neighbourhood, with its cobbled streets and pastel-painted Cape Malay houses, is one of Africa's most photographed quarters, and the Company's Garden at the foot of the mountain traces Cape Town's origins to 1652. A Table Mountain Aerial Cableway ride — best booked online to skip queues — rewards with views from Robben Island to the Winelands on a clear morning.

The Cape Winelands — Stellenbosch, Franschhoek, and Paarl — lie 45–60 minutes from the city and harbour South Africa's oldest Cape Dutch homesteads alongside world-class chenin blanc, pinotage, and pinot noir. Franschhoek's main street hosts some of the country's most celebrated restaurants; the Wine Tram is an easy circuit through four estates. For those with more time, the Cape Peninsula drive around Chapman's Peak to the Cape of Good Hope Nature Reserve and Boulders Beach penguin colony is a full day well spent — one of the world's great coastal drives.
bullets: Table Mountain Cableway: pre-book at tablemountain.net — closes in strong wind; check weather before setting out
Stellenbosch Wine Route: 200+ estates; best explored by bicycle, wine tram, or with a designated driver
Robben Island: ferry from V&A Waterfront; book in advance at robben-island.org.za — sells out weeks ahead
Boulders Beach penguins: 15-min walk in the colony; entry fee applies; Cape Peninsula day circuit
Chapman's Peak Drive: occasionally closes for rockfall maintenance — check before committing to the route

sections.title: Kruger Safari
sections.body:
Kruger National Park covers 19,485km² — approximately the size of Wales — stretching along the Mozambique border through Limpopo and Mpumalanga provinces. It harbours Africa's densest concentration of publicly accessible Big Five wildlife, with over 500 bird species and nearly 3,000km of self-drive road. The southern camps (Skukuza, Lower Sabie, Berg-en-Dal) are generally most productive for leopard, lion, and rhino, while the quieter far north around Shingwedzi and Pafuri offers wilderness solitude and exceptional birding including Pel's fishing owl.

Self-driving Kruger is straightforward: main roads are tar, loop roads are gravel, speed limits are 50km/h (strictly enforced), and you set your own pace. Gates open at sunrise and close at sunset — latecomers face substantial fines. Night drives led by SANParks rangers operate from major camps. For immersive foot experiences, book a multi-day wilderness trail on foot with a certified guide (maximum 8 guests; months-ahead booking essential). The private reserves on Kruger's western boundary — Sabi Sand, Timbavati, Thornybush — offer luxury lodge safaris with off-road access. Leopard sightings at Sabi Sand are near-daily.
bullets: Book SANParks camps via sanparks.org — opens 11 months ahead; Skukuza and Lower Sabie fill within minutes
Sunrise gate entry is essential: predators are most active before 9am; arrive at the gate before it opens
Private reserves (Sabi Sand, Timbavati): luxury all-inclusive from R5,000–R30,000+ pps/night; off-road access
3-day wilderness trails: guided on foot with SANParks — apply months ahead; transformative experience
Malaria prophylaxis recommended for Kruger; consult your doctor 4–6 weeks before travel

sections.title: Garden Route
sections.body:
The Garden Route sweeps along South Africa's southeastern coast for roughly 300km from Mossel Bay to Storms River — a succession of indigenous forests, turquoise lagoons, dramatic cliffs, and small harbour towns. The Outeniqua Mountains form a dark-green backdrop and the Indian Ocean glitters to the south. Knysna, with its famous lagoon and the Heads, is the emotional heart of the route; the Knysna Forest hikes around Diepwalle and the old-growth yellowwood trees are highlights. Plettenberg Bay combines upmarket beach accommodation with an extraordinary concentration of marine life: southern right whales (August–November), bottlenose dolphins, Bryde's whales, and Cape fur seals.

The Tsitsikamma National Park at the eastern end contains the Storms River mouth suspension bridge gorge walk — one of South Africa's most rewarding short hikes, taking under an hour and completely free with park entry. The world's highest commercial bungee jump (216m) operates from Bloukrans Bridge nearby. George and Wilderness make useful bases on the western end, with scheduled flights from Cape Town and Johannesburg. A short inland detour to Oudtshoorn in the Klein Karoo opens up the Cango Caves, ostrich farms, and the Swartberg Pass — one of the country's finest mountain drives.
bullets: Knysna: book accommodation well ahead; completely packed December–January; visit in May for best balance
Bloukrans Bungee: 216m world record jump; walk-ins accepted at faceadrenalin.co.za; book online to save time
Tsitsikamma: Storms River suspension bridge is a free short walk with park entry — don't skip it
Whale watching, Plettenberg Bay: best Aug–Nov; Offshore Adventures and Ocean Blue both reliable operators
Otter Trail (5 days coastal): South Africa's most sought-after trail — book 12 months ahead at sanparks.org

sections.title: Visa & Safety
sections.body:
South Africa is straightforward for most Western visitors. UK, US, EU, Australian, and Canadian passport holders receive 90-day visa-free tourism entry — no advance application required. Your passport must have at least 30 days validity beyond your departure date and at least two consecutive blank pages for entry stamps. A critical requirement for families: children under 18 travelling with one parent, or unaccompanied by both parents, must carry an unabridged (full) birth certificate at all South African entry and exit points. This is strictly enforced and can result in being turned around — no exceptions. If in doubt, carry the document.

Safety in South Africa is real and manageable with common-sense precautions. Some urban areas — particularly parts of Johannesburg CBD, Cape Town's outlying neighbourhoods, and certain townships after dark — have higher crime rates than most visitor nations. In practice: keep valuables out of sight in cars, use ATMs inside shopping centres rather than on street corners, avoid stopping at isolated roadside rest stops at night, and trust your instincts. Tourist areas like the V&A Waterfront, Stellenbosch, Franschhoek, and all national parks and private reserves are safe and well-managed. Crime against tourists in Kruger, the Winelands, and the Garden Route is extremely rare.
bullets: UK, US, EU, AU, CA: 90 days visa-free; passport valid 30+ days beyond departure; two blank pages required
Children under 18: unabridged birth certificate required — strictly enforced at all South African ports of entry
Yellow fever certificate: required if arriving directly from a yellow fever endemic country
Johannesburg: use Sandton and Rosebank for accommodation; avoid the CBD after dark and leave nothing in cars
Travel insurance strongly recommended — South African private medical care is excellent but very expensive

sections.title: Where to Stay
sections.body:
South Africa covers the full accommodation spectrum from rough-and-ready campsites to landmark five-star city hotels. Cape Town and the Winelands have an exceptional range of boutique guesthouses, private villa rentals, and design hotels — the Cape Dutch homesteads of Franschhoek and Stellenbosch are among Africa's most atmospheric stays, many with their own vineyards and award-winning restaurants. For city breaks in Johannesburg, Sandton and Rosebank are the recommended areas, with solid international hotels close to Apartheid Museum (the world's best museum of its kind), Vilakazi Street, and Melville's restaurants.

In and around Kruger, SANParks rest camps deliver clean, fenced accommodation from around R400 per campsite to R2,500+ for a fully equipped chalet with kitchen. Bungalows inside the national park are enormously popular with South African families for self-catering holidays. On the Garden Route, Plettenberg Bay has premium beachside resorts; Knysna offers excellent lakeside villas for self-catering. Throughout the country, private apartment and villa rentals offer excellent value for groups of four or more. For pure wilderness, South Africa's Wilderness Trail huts inside Kruger and Cape Nature's park huts in the Cederberg are unforgettable.
bullets: SANParks rest camps: book at sanparks.org up to 11 months ahead — school holiday camps fill in minutes
Cape Winelands: boutique farm stays and Cape Dutch homesteads at Stellenbosch, Franschhoek, and Paarl
Johannesburg: Sandton and Rosebank are the safest and most convenient neighbourhoods for visitors
Private game lodges (Sabi Sand, Timbavati, Phinda): premium all-inclusive from R5,000+ pps/night
Self-catering on the Garden Route: excellent value at Knysna, Wilderness, and Plettenberg Bay

sections.title: Okavango Delta
sections.body:
The Okavango is one of the world's great natural phenomena — an inland river system that pours down from the Angolan highlands and fans out into a shallow alluvial delta covering up to 22,000km² in the northern Kalahari basin. There is no outlet to the sea; the water evaporates and percolates over months. The annual flood from Angolan rains arrives in Botswana between June and August — precisely the dry season — transforming the delta into a shimmering maze of papyrus-lined channels, lily-covered lagoons, and isolated islands. Wildlife concentrates as the surrounding Kalahari dries out: elephant, buffalo, hippo, red lechwe, and Africa's densest lion and wild dog populations converge in the permanent water areas.

The classic experience is a three-night stay at a fly-in camp in the permanent Delta — Chief's Island, Xigera, or the Nxabeu concession — arriving by small bush plane from Maun. The mokoro, a traditional dugout pole canoe, provides a uniquely silent way to explore shallow channels, drifting within metres of hippos and water monitors. Most camps combine morning game drives, mokoro excursions, and guided walks on islands for a three-dimensional wildlife experience. Budget travellers can access the Delta edge from Maun by vehicle and take a mokoro day trip, though the deeper private concessions remain the gold standard.
bullets: Best flood levels for mokoro and wildlife: July–August; book fly-in camps 6–12 months ahead
Chief's Island (Moremi): legendary predator territory — best wild dog, lion, and leopard area in the Delta
Mokoro excursions usually included in all-inclusive lodge rates; day trips bookable independently from Maun
Maun is the gateway — fly OR Tambo or Johannesburg to Maun via Air Botswana or Airlink
Private concession camps strictly limit guest numbers to protect the ecosystem; fees are substantial but justified

sections.title: Chobe River
sections.body:
Chobe National Park in northern Botswana is famous above all for elephant — herds of 500 or more have been documented here during the dry season, making it Africa's highest-density elephant range. The Chobe Riverfront provides exceptional and easily accessible game viewing; afternoon river cruises and morning 4x4 drives are both rewarding throughout the year, with the dry season (May–October) producing the greatest concentrations. The park also holds significant lion, leopard, spotted hyena, and buffalo numbers alongside an extraordinary waterbird spectacle including African skimmer, open-billed stork, and the sentinel-like fish eagle.

Kasane, the small gateway town at the Chobe Riverfront, sits at the intersection of four countries — Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, and Namibia — making it an ideal base for a Victoria Falls circuit. The Kazungula Bridge, opened 2021, has dramatically cut crossing times between Botswana and Zambia compared to the old pontoon. The Chobe day trip from Victoria Falls is one of Southern Africa's most popular excursions: a short drive to Kasane and an afternoon boat cruise puts you among elephant, hippo, and crocodile before returning to the Falls by early evening. Park entry fees are paid at the gate and are priced in Pula or USD.
bullets: Best game viewing: late dry season (Aug–Oct) for maximum wildlife concentration around the Chobe River
Chobe riverfront lodges in Kasane: wide range from budget guesthouses to the landmark Chobe Game Lodge
Sunset boat cruise: essential; book through your lodge or Kasane boat operators — 2.5 hours on the water
Victoria Falls day trip to Chobe: popular and easy — confirm whether park fees are included in the tour price
Kazungula Bridge: no more pontoon delays; drive between Zambia and Botswana in minutes

sections.title: Makgadikgadi
sections.body:
The Makgadikgadi Pans stretch across northeastern Botswana as one of the world's largest salt flats — a remnant of an ancient super-lake that once covered most of the Kalahari basin. In the dry season (April–September), the pans are crispy, blindingly white, and completely flat to every horizon: a completely alien moonscape where quad bikes are the only objects that break the line. At night, the total absence of light pollution turns the sky into a full planetarium above cracked, silent earth. Meerkats, brown hyena, and gemsbok survive in these inhospitable margins, adapted to the mineral-rich fringe of the salt.

The green season transformation is equally dramatic. When the rains arrive (December–March), shallow floodwater covers the southern pans and draws one of Africa's last great wildlife spectacles: the zebra migration — up to 35,000 animals moving between the Delta and the pans in a circuit that mirrors the ancient patterns of the now-vanished lake. Flamingos gather in extraordinary numbers to breed on the flooded salt crust when conditions are right. The Makgadikgadi and Nxai Pan National Parks flank the pans and offer self-drive access; Jack's Camp near Gweta remains the iconic luxury base.
bullets: Zebra migration (Dec–Mar): one of Africa's last great land migrations; Jack's Camp for the guided experience
Dry season (Apr–Sep): otherworldly landscape for quad biking and unrivalled southern hemisphere stargazing
Flamingo breeding: December–February at Sowa Pan when flood levels are sufficient
Nxai Pan (north): green season concentrations of zebra, springbok, and lion — self-drive accessible
Self-drive: tarred road to Gweta; 4x4 and navigation confidence required beyond the main road

sections.title: Fly-in vs Self-Drive
sections.body:
Botswana's premier wilderness areas — the deep Okavango Delta, Linyanti, and Selinda — are accessible only by small charter aircraft or after many hours on 4x4-only sandy tracks. The fly-in versus self-drive question comes down to time, budget, and experience. Fly-in safaris are the default for international first-timers: a 15–45-minute bush flight from Maun deposits you directly at a remote camp where everything — meals, drinks, activities, park fees — is covered in the all-inclusive daily rate. The experience is seamless, deeply immersive, and completely focused on wildlife.

Self-drive access is practical in Moremi Game Reserve (4x4 essential), the Chobe Riverfront (accessible by 2WD from Kasane), and the Makgadikgadi Pans. The Central Kalahari Game Reserve — one of the largest protected areas on Earth — is accessible by self-drive but demands a high-clearance 4x4, sufficient fuel (200km between fuel points), and solid navigation skills. A two-week self-drive loop from Johannesburg combining the Chobe Riverfront and Moremi gives tremendous freedom at a fraction of the fly-in cost. Campsites inside Moremi and Chobe are basic but bookable in advance through the Department of Wildlife.
bullets: Fly-in: Maun to Delta camps 15–45 min; all-inclusive lodge rates typically USD 400–1,500+ pps/night
Self-drive Moremi: 4x4 only; sandy tracks; camp bookable at dwnp.gov.bw
Chobe Riverfront: accessible in a 2WD from Kasane; daily park entry fees apply
Central Kalahari: 4x4 only; carry 200L of fuel; limited phone signal; very remote experience
Combination trip: Kasane (2 nights) → fly-in Delta (3 nights) → Maun → Makgadikgadi (2 nights) is a classic circuit

sections.title: Entry & Visa
sections.body:
Botswana is one of Southern Africa's most visitor-friendly destinations for international travellers. UK, US, EU, Australian, and Canadian passport holders all receive 90-day visa-free entry on arrival at any designated port of entry — no advance application or fee required. South African passport holders are also visa-free, and SADC nationals generally receive visa-free entry though days permitted can vary by nationality. There is no e-visa system for Botswana; entry permission is granted on arrival with a valid passport.

Yellow fever vaccination is required if you are arriving from a yellow fever endemic country. Malaria prophylaxis is strongly recommended for the Okavango Delta, Chobe, and all of northern Botswana year-round — the disease is endemic in these areas, transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes. Your passport should be valid for at least six months beyond your entry date with at least one blank visa page. Daily wildlife concession and national park fees in the Okavango area are built into lodge rates for fly-in guests, but self-drivers pay at park gates in Pula or by card.
bullets: UK, US, EU, AU, CA: 90 days visa-free on arrival at any designated entry point — no e-visa required
South African and most SADC passport holders: visa-free — confirm permitted days at gov.bw
Malaria prophylaxis: strongly recommended for Delta, Chobe, and northern Botswana year-round
Yellow fever certificate required if arriving from endemic countries
Self-drive park fees: pay at the gate in Pula or by Visa card; lodge guests have fees included
